newsReadings.title: The Hidden Power Bill of Artificial Intelligence
newsReadings.source: International Energy Agency, World Energy Outlook 2026 (reported by Tom's Hardware, 19 November 2026)
newsReadings.passage:
Artificial intelligence is frequently portrayed as weightless: a chatbot that answers in seconds, a model that conjures images from a sentence, a system that lives, invisibly, in the cloud. Yet behind every prompt lies a physical reality of concrete, copper and current. The vast warehouses of computers that train and run AI systems consume electricity on a scale that was, until recently, the preserve of heavy industry. Now, according to the International Energy Agency's World Energy Outlook 2026, that appetite is about to reshape the world's power system.

The Agency's central finding is stark. Electricity demand from data centres is set to double by 2030, driven overwhelmingly by artificial intelligence, and the investment behind it is immense: some $4 trillion in planned spending on new facilities. Around 120 gigawatts of data-centre capacity already exists worldwide; another 120 gigawatts is due to be completed by the end of the decade, and three-quarters of it will be dedicated to AI. To put that growth in perspective, the Agency calculates that it is roughly equivalent to adding an entire Great Britain to global electricity demand within a few short years.

Several forces are converging to produce this surge. Training a frontier AI model — the months-long process of teaching a system to recognise patterns in trillions of words and images — can consume as much electricity as a small town uses in a year. But training is no longer the main driver. Inference, the everyday business of answering billions of user queries, now accounts for a growing share of consumption, and unlike training, it never pauses. Data centres run around the clock, their processors generating prodigious amounts of heat that must in turn be removed by energy-hungry cooling systems. Moreover, the most powerful facilities tend to cluster together, in a handful of regions with cheap land and fast fibre-optic connections, concentrating their demand on local grids that were never designed for such loads.

The consequences for electricity networks are already visible. In several countries, grid operators have warned that connection queues for new data centres stretch years into the future, and some large projects have been delayed or relocated because the local network simply cannot supply them. Where supply is tight, prices rise, and households and manufacturers find themselves competing, indirectly, with server farms for the same electrons. The irony is acute: the technology industry, which has long presented itself as the champion of a clean-energy future, has become one of the fastest-growing sources of new electricity demand. In some regions, the strain has prompted an uncomfortable debate about priorities — whether a new data centre should be permitted to connect before homes and hospitals whose needs have waited longer in the same queue.

How the world responds will determine whether this boom becomes a climate liability or an opportunity. The Agency notes that data-centre operators are among the largest buyers of renewable electricity, and many new facilities are being sited beside wind and solar farms, or near hydroelectric dams. Nuclear power, long out of favour, is experiencing a revival as technology companies seek the steady, carbon-free output that reactors provide. Engineers are also squeezing more work from each watt: more efficient chips, better cooling, and software that shifts computation to times and places where clean power is abundant.

Nevertheless, the fundamental question remains unanswered. The demand is arriving faster than new clean generation can be built, and in the interim, some grids are leaning more heavily on gas and coal to keep the servers running. The IEA's message is therefore not that artificial intelligence should be restrained, but that the energy transition must accelerate to match it. The cloud may feel weightless, but its power bill is very real — and it is coming due.

questions.q: According to the IEA's World Energy Outlook 2026, what is expected to happen to data-centre electricity demand by 2030?

It will fall as chips become more efficient.

Billions of user queries must be answered continuously, around the clock.

newsReadings.title: Climate Disasters Are Reaching Children Faster Than Ever
newsReadings.source: Save the Children analysis, released 9 November 2026 (published on ReliefWeb); World Meteorological Organization, State of the Climate report, November 2026
newsReadings.passage:
When the COP31 United Nations climate conference opened in Antalya, Türkiye, on 9 November 2026, the delegates were greeted not with a diplomatic statement but with a number. An average of 330 million children a year were exposed to severe climate disasters — heatwaves, droughts, tropical cyclones and extreme rainfall — between January 2022 and September 2026, according to new analysis by Save the Children. That figure is nearly 50 per cent higher than the 222 million a year recorded in the preceding five years, and it makes the youngest generation the clearest measure of a warming world.

The scale of the increase is difficult to absorb. In the first nine months of 2026 alone, about 205 million children experienced a severe climate event, and because the data runs only to September, the charity expects the full-year total to be higher still. Over the longer span, one in three children worldwide — 911 million in all — have been exposed to climate disasters of some severity since 2022, a rise of 17 per cent on the previous five-year period. These are not projections of a distant future; they are a record of what has already happened to children alive today.

Children bear a disproportionate share of the harm, and the reasons are both physiological and social. Young bodies are less able to regulate temperature during heatwaves, and more vulnerable to the diseases that follow floods and droughts. Beyond the body, the disruption is cumulative: schools close, harvests fail, families are displaced, and nutrition and healthcare are interrupted at precisely the ages when they matter most. As Save the Children's analysis emphasises, the youngest and the poorest are paying the highest price for a crisis they did least to cause.

No region has been spared, but the geography of exposure in 2026 surprised many observers. Western Europe was the worst-affected region, where one out of every two children faced severe weather events amid a succession of record-breaking heatwaves that made it the region's hottest summer on record. The finding undercuts a persistent assumption that climate disasters are a problem confined to distant, vulnerable places. The World Meteorological Organization, in its State of the Climate report released on the same day, confirmed that 2026 is on track to be one of the four hottest years ever recorded, and is likely to tie with 2024 as the warmest.

The timing of the release was deliberate. COP31, which runs until 20 November and brings together nearly 200 countries, is the forum where governments negotiate emissions cuts, adaptation finance and support for the countries least able to cope. By publishing on the opening day, Save the Children sought to ensure that negotiators confronted, in hard numbers, what warming is already doing to children before they began two weeks of talks. The charity's argument is that adaptation — early warning systems, heat-resilient schools, climate-proofed health services — is not a secondary concern but a matter of immediate protection. Yet adaptation funding has consistently fallen short of what is needed, and the gap between promises made at previous summits and money actually delivered remains one of the most contentious issues on the conference agenda.

Whether the conference delivers on that agenda remains to be seen, but the data has already reframed the debate. For years, climate change was discussed largely in terms of degrees of warming and tonnes of carbon. The new analysis translates those abstractions into a human ledger: hundreds of millions of childhoods interrupted, year after year, at a rate half as high again as it was five years ago. If the purpose of the climate negotiations is to protect the future, the evidence suggests that the future is already arriving — and that it is arriving first for children.

notes.meaning: 重新界定；换个角度看待

options: About 330 million children a year were exposed to severe climate disasters between January 2022 and September 2026, nearly 50% more than in the previous five years.
The number of children affected by climate disasters has fallen since the Paris Agreement.
Most climate disasters now affect adults rather than children.
Western Europe has been unaffected by severe climate events.

Why are children particularly vulnerable during heatwaves, according to the passage?
options: They spend more time outdoors than adults.
Their bodies are less able to regulate temperature.
They are more likely to live near the coast.
They receive less warning of extreme weather.
